newsitem.title: TANZANIA: 15,000 Rwandans abandon camps in Tanzania - U.N.
newsitem.headline: 15,000 Rwandans abandon camps in Tanzania - U.N.

text.p: About 15,000 Rwandan refugees have abandoned two camps in northwestern Tanzania, possibly to avoid being repatriated under a Tanzanian government campaign, a U.N. official said on Monday.
U.N. refugee agency (UNHCR) spokesman Peter Kessler said most of the refugees made off into the bush on Sunday heading north and northeast, away from the Rwandan border.

The exodus bodes ill for the repatriation plan for the 542,000 Rwandan refugees in Tanzania and it could end in bands of Rwandans wandering around the country, as has happened in Zaire on the other side of Rwanda.

Kessler said it was hard to guess at the motives and intentions of the refugees but he linked their flight to the presence in the camps of the Interahamwe, the Hutu extremist militia which does not want the refugees to go home.

The Interahamwe played a major role in the massacre of up to one million Rwandan Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda in 1994. Many of them fear going home because they might face prosecution for their part in the genocide of Tutsis.

"They (the refugees) have been under pressure from Interahamwe and so-called refugee leaders to ignore the Tanzanian government and not to go home. They (the Interahamwe) have been knocking on every hut, terrorising the refugees with scare stories about the situation back home," Kessler said.
He said he could not rule out some refugees wanting to move away from Interahamwe influence and go home in peace.
Aid workers in Tanzania said the refugees refused to discuss their destination.
"It seems clear that some intimidators are actively trying to persuade refugees not to go home," one aid official added.
UNHCR and the Tanzanian government have given the Rwandan refugees in western Tanzania until the end of this month to go home. They have not said what will happen to those who refuse.

Kessler said the refugees, 8,000 from the Rubwera camp and 7,000 from Kigenyi camp, violated a Tanzanian rule that refugees should not stray far from the camps. "They (the Tanzanians) will not look kindly on these movements," he added.
The UNHCR denied reports that the two camps, which originally held about 40,000 Rwandans, had emptied.
The human rights group Amnesty International has criticised the repatriation plan, saying UNHCR was condoning what amounted to forced repatriation.
Kessler said more than 5,500 refugees at other camps near Ngara had signed up for repatriation and thousands of them would probably move on Monday and Tuesday.
Hundreds of those lined up on Sunday in driving rain at the Benaco camp, with 160,000 inhabitants the largest in Tanzania, to register to go back to Rwanda.
The refugees said they had decided to return in a block to ensure their safety, but aid workers say a split in the camps is likely, with some unwilling to go back because of the genocide.
"I am not certain that it will be safe back in Rwanda but all of my people are trying to go back now," said Eugene Bujirimana, 26, from Kibungo province.
"I came here because Rwanda was at war but now I want to go home because if I don't go home now I may be here for a very long time," said Claudine Kambawazi.
